newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: UAE, worried over Iran, signs British defence pact.
newsitem.headline: UAE, worried over Iran, signs British defence pact.

text.p: Britain and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday signed a defence cooperation accord which pledged British help to deter aggression if the oil-rich Gulf state, nervous about an Iranian arms buildup, is threatened.
Years of negotiations ended with the signatures of British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo and the UAE's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Sheikh Hamdan bin Zaid al-Nahayan.

Portillo, on a few hours' flying visit, said the pact was a significant event in Britain's defence relationship with the UAE -- the former Trucial States which depended upon British protection for 150 years until independence in 1971.

"We have a long-standing friendship with the UAE, and I very much hope that this accord will allow us to extend defence cooperation still further to the benefit of both our countries and of the security and stability of the Gulf region as a whole," he said.

As Portillo spoke at a news conference at the British embassy in the UAE capital, Iran's armed forces were engaged in 10 days of war games involving 100 ships and 40 aircrafts in the Gulf, conduit for 15 million barrels of oil exports each day.
Iran's naval power is enhanced by two Russian submarines and a third left a Russian port earlier this week for the Gulf.
The sparsely-populated UAE is in dispute with the Islamic republic over three islands close to shipping lanes near the strategic Strait of Hormuz at the entrance to the Gulf.
It is particularly worried about its much larger neighbour's acquisition of modern weaponry.
The UAE and its five partners in the Gulf Cooperation Council earlier this year said Iran's plans to acquire ever more sophisticated arms posed a threat to the region.
Portillo, who also had talks with the chief of staff of the UAE's 57,000-man armed forces Sheikh Mohammed bin Zaid, said the timing of the accord and the Iranian war games was coincidental.
"We have had extensive discussions on Gulf security today and there have been no areas of disagreement between us in those discussions," he said.

Portillo said exact terms of the accord, which he described as "quite precise and quite frank", were confidential but Britain was concerned about the security of its friends in the Gulf from every point of view.

"The accord covers training and exercise training. It covers the development together of a deterrent so as to ensure there is no aggression against the United Arab Emirates. It allows us to draw up joint military plans and in certain circumstances to implement those joint military plans in the event of an aggression against the UAE," he said.

Portillo said there was no commitment to send a specific number of British troops to the UAE's aid, unlike an agreement Abu Dhabi signed with France last December which pledged to rush a 70,000-man rapid reaction force to the Gulf.
"What the agreement commits us to now is working out joint plans and we would like to get on with that beginning in the next few days," he said.
Lieutenant General Hew Pike, Britain's leading military expert on the Middle East, would be in Abu Dhabi within a few days to supervise planning.
Portillo said differences over which laws would apply to British troops in the UAE had been settled by agreement on joint jurisdiction.
British defence contractors have been hoping the accord would lead to more UAE business but Portillo said there was nothing in the agreement about defence deals at all.

He could not think of any specific contracts pending but he said British companies -- Vosper Thorneycroft, Racal Electronics and British Aerospace -- had been successful in making UAE sales in the past and Britain wished to see its friends properly equipped so they could provide their own deterrence and their own defence.
